summary:
Ceuta, an autonomous city of Spain, stands under the national framework: it has no LGTBI or gender-identity statute of its own. The legislative index at planlgtbi.es states expressly that Ceuta and Melilla must apply the national equality framework and central-government policies in the absence of a regional law, and FELGTBI+'s September 2025 radiography of LGTBI+ policy, prepared with the Universidad de Salamanca, records Asturias, Castilla y León, Ceuta and Melilla as the only Spanish territories still without a specific law on the promotion of LGTBI+ rights. The Spanish national statute therefore supplies the whole of the visitor-facing protection regime in Ceuta.

Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16. Legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Spain. This contrasts with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

Other operative provisions of the national statute include a ban on non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, expanded assisted reproduction rules, parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthened sexuality education, and anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force since 2005.

There is no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately. Both are mainland cases illustrating how the national provisions are applied.

Protection machinery in Ceuta is currently exercised through civil-society channels as well as the state. On 17 September 2026 Europa Press reported that the LGTBI+ association Arcópoli wrote to the Secretary of State for Migration, Pilar Cancela, demanding the urgent transfer to the peninsula of LGTBI+ migrants remaining in Ceuta after thousands entered irregularly on 30 and 31 July. Arcópoli called transfer the only effective measure to guarantee their protection and inclusion, cited the extreme vulnerability of people who flee criminalisation and persecution in countries including Morocco, and launched a free remote social, psychological and legal support service for those in Ceuta.

Comparatively, Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 23-country survey ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline predating the 2023 law.
tangentialFactors:
The single-sex-space rules a trans visitor will encounter in Ceuta are set in Madrid, not in Ceuta's own administration, and they follow the legal gender marker rather than biological sex. Travellers arriving from or comparing with the United Kingdom should expect a materially different basis for facility access.

The statutory gap is a standing feature rather than a transient one. FELGTBI+'s September 2025 report notes legislative progress in Castilla y León and Asturias in June 2025 and records no equivalent step for Ceuta or Melilla, leaving Ceuta in the inventory as a case with no regional LGTBI or gender-identity law more than two and a half years after the national statute entered into force.

A 2020 precedent study had placed Ceuta and Melilla at the tail of trans-student recognition and protection rankings among Spanish territories, a baseline that predates both the 2023 national law and the 2025 report and that is not restated with updated figures in the sources.

The mass irregular entry into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July 2026 and the subsequent association correspondence mark Ceuta as a site of acute pressure on LGBTI+ protection, with the vulnerability cited being flight from criminalisation and persecution in a neighbouring country rather than risk created inside Ceuta itself.

The comparative ranking drawn from the 2016 23-country survey is a dated baseline that predates the 2023 law; it indicates long-standing public support for self-declaration but does not measure conditions after the statute.

outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records an Article 43 gender-marker rectification granted or refused by a Civil Registry in Ceuta, and none documents facility-access disputes, healthcare refusals or discrimination complaints filed within Ceuta under Ley 4/2023. Enforcement examples in the inventory come from Vigo and Valencia on the mainland.

The outcome of Arcópoli's letter to the Secretary State for Migration is not stated: whether any transfers of LGTBI+ migrants out of Ceuta were authorised after 17 September 2026 remains unresolved in these sources, as does the number of LGTBI+ migrants said to remain in Ceuta.

The 2020 trans-student recognition and protection ranking that places Ceuta and Melilla last is described as a precedent study; no updated figure for Ceuta after the 2023 national law appears in the inventory, so the current position of Ceuta on that measure is not sourced here.

Whether Ceuta's municipal or autonomous-city administration has adopted implementing measures, guidance or complaint channels under the national LGTBI statute is not addressed by any source listed, and no Ceuta-specific hate-crime or gender-identity aggravation case is recorded.
